original_value: Multiobjective evolutionary algorithms (MOEAs) have progressed significantly in recent decades, but most of them are designed to solve unconstrained multiobjective optimization problems. In fact, many real-world multiobjective problems contain a number of constraints. To promote research on constrained multiobjective optimization, we first propose a problem classification scheme with three primary types of difficulty, which reflect various types of challenges presented by real-world optimization problems, in order to characterize the constraint functions in constrained multiobjective optimization problems (CMOPs). These are feasibility-hardness, convergence-hardness, and diversity-hardness. We then develop a general toolkit to construct difficulty adjustable and scalable CMOPs (DAS-CMOPs, or DAS-CMaOPs when the number of objectives is greater than three) with three types of parameterized constraint functions developed to capture the three proposed types of difficulty. In fact, the combination of the three primary constraint functions with different parameters allows the construction of a large variety of CMOPs, with difficulty that can be defined by a triplet, with each of its parameters specifying the level of one of the types of primary difficulty. Furthermore, the number of objectives in this toolkit can be scaled beyond three. Based on this toolkit, we suggest nine difficulty adjustable and scalable CMOPs and nine CMaOPs, to be called DAS-CMOP1-9 and DAS-CMaOP1-9, respectively. To evaluate the proposed test problems, two popular CMOEAs—MOEA/D-CDP (MOEA/D with constraint dominance principle) and NSGA-II-CDP (NSGA-II with constraint dominance principle) and two popular constrained many-objective evolutionary algorithms (CMaOEAs)—C-MOEA/DD and C-NSGA-III—are used to compare performance on DAS-CMOP1-9 and DAS-CMaOP1-9 with a variety of difficulty triplets, respectively. The experimental results reveal that mechanisms in MOEA/D-CDP may be more effective in solving convergence-hard DAS-CMOPs, while mechanisms of NSGA-II-CDP may be more effective in solving DAS-CMOPs with simultaneous diversity-, feasibility-, and convergence-hardness. Mechanisms in C-NSGA-III may be more effective in solving feasibility-hard CMaOPs, while mechanisms of C-MOEA/DD may be more effective in solving CMaOPs with convergence-hardness. In addition, none of them can solve these problems efficiently, which stimulates us to continue to develop new CMOEAs and CMaOEAs to solve the suggested DAS-CMOPs and DAS-CMaOPs.

result.paraphrase: Multiobjective evolutionary algorithms (MOEAs) have advanced markedly in recent decades, yet most are intended for unconstrained multiobjective optimization problems. In practice, many real-world multiobjective problems include numerous constraints. To encourage research in constrained multiobjective optimization, we first introduce a problem classification scheme with three main difficulty types that capture the kinds of challenges posed by real-world optimization problems, for characterizing constraint functions in constrained multiobjective optimization problems (CMOPs). These are feasibility-hardness, convergence-hardness, and diversity-hardness. We then build a general toolkit for constructing difficulty-adjustable and scalable CMOPs (DAS-CMOPs, or DAS-CMaOPs when the number of objectives exceeds three) using three parameterized constraint-function types designed to represent the three proposed difficulty types. In fact, combining the three primary constraint functions with different parameter settings enables a wide range of CMOPs to be created, with difficulty specified by a triplet whose parameters indicate the level of each primary difficulty type. Moreover, this toolkit can scale the number of objectives beyond three. Based on it, we propose nine difficulty-adjustable and scalable CMOPs and nine CMaOPs, called DAS-CMOP1-9 and DAS-CMaOP1-9, respectively. To assess the proposed test problems, two widely used CMOEAs—MOEA/D-CDP (MOEA/D with constraint dominance principle) and NSGA-II-CDP (NSGA-II with constraint dominance principle)—and two popular constrained many-objective evolutionary algorithms (CMaOEAs)—C-MOEA/DD and C-NSGA-III—are employed to compare performance on DAS-CMOP1-9 and DAS-CMaOP1-9 under various difficulty triplets, respectively. The experimental results show that the mechanisms in MOEA/D-CDP may be more effective for solving convergence-hard DAS-CMOPs, whereas those in NSGA-II-CDP may be more effective for DAS-CMOPs that exhibit simultaneous diversity-, feasibility-, and convergence-hardness. The mechanisms in C-NSGA-III may be more effective for feasibility-hard CMaOPs, while those in C-MOEA/DD may be more effective for CMaOPs with convergence-hardness. In addition, none of these methods can solve the problems efficiently, motivating further development of new CMOEAs and CMaOEAs to tackle the proposed DAS-CMOPs and DAS-CMaOPs.
